opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's shaped it quite a lot, actually. A lot of us spent years working on embodied AI, so things like navigation in simulated homes, instruction following, agents that have to perceive an environment, take actions, and deal with the consequences of those actions over long horizons. When we started thinking about web agents, it struck us how similar the core problems are. The browser is an environment. You get an observation, which might be a screenshot or the DOM or some mix of the two. You take an action like clicking, typing, or scrolling. The world changes, and you have to keep going until the task is done.

So a few lessons carried over pretty directly. The first is that evaluation in realistic environments really matters. In embodied AI we learned early that static datasets only get you so far. You need interactive benchmarks where the agent actually has to act and recover from its own mistakes, because errors compound. The same is true on the web. An agent that's 90% accurate per step can still fail most multi-step tasks.

The second is how important simulation and scale are. In embodied work, a lot of progress came once we could run huge numbers of episodes in simulators. For web agents, the equivalent is having lots of sandboxed environments, realistic sites and workflows, where agents can practice, explore, and generate training signal without breaking anything in the real world.

The third is robustness and generalization. In embodied AI you'd train in some set of houses and then test in houses you'd never seen, and that gap was always the humbling part. The web has the same issue, maybe even more so. Every site is laid out differently, things change constantly, and there are pop-ups, logins, and edge cases everywhere. So we think a lot about agents that can handle novelty instead of memorizing particular interfaces.

And honestly, the biggest shift in perspective is that the web is a far more practical place to deploy these ideas today. With physical robots, hardware and the messiness of the real world slow everything down. On the web, the "body" is the browser, and you can get agents doing useful things for people much sooner. That's a big part of why it's so exciting to us. It feels like a place where a lot of what we learned in embodied AI can actually turn into something people use every day.

r001.rationale: It says web agents observe the browser, take actions, and deal with resulting changes over long horizons, directly linking consequential sequential decisions to embodied AI.

r002.rationale: It contrasts web agents with physical robots, saying hardware and real-world messiness slow deployment, while browser-based agents can be deployed sooner.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's influenced it a lot, actually. For years my group was working on embodied AI, so things like Habitat, where you have an agent in a simulated 3D environment, it has to navigate to a goal, follow an instruction, find an object, that kind of thing. And when we started looking at web agents, my first reaction was, this is the same problem. The browser is the environment. The agent perceives a state, which is the page, it takes an action, clicking or typing or scrolling, the state changes, and it has to keep doing that over a long horizon to accomplish something a person asked for.

So a lot of the lessons carried over directly. One is that long-horizon sequential decision making is hard in a way that single-shot prediction just isn't. Errors compound. If you take one wrong turn in a house, you end up in the wrong room, and if you click the wrong link, you end up in the wrong part of a website, and now you have to realize that and recover. So we spent a lot of time in embodied AI thinking about exploration, about memory, about knowing when you're lost, and all of that shows up again.

Another one is the importance of simulators and benchmarks. In embodied AI we couldn't have made progress without photorealistic, fast simulators where you can run millions of episodes. The web is interesting because in some sense the environment already exists, but it's also live, it changes, actions have real consequences. So you still want sandboxed, reproducible environments to train and evaluate in, and the gap between the sandbox and the real web is very analogous to the sim-to-real gap we worried about with robots.

And then the thing that's different, which has been humbling, is that the action space on the web is much more semantic. In navigation your actions are turn left, move forward. On the web, the right action depends on reading and understanding language, understanding intent, understanding what a form field is for. So the perception and language side matters a lot more, and that's where large language and vision-language models have changed what's possible. The embodied work taught us how to think about the agent loop, and the foundation models gave us the perception to make that loop actually work on something as messy as a website.

r001.rationale: The response says embodied AI and web agents both involve long-horizon sequential decisions: agents act, the environment changes, and errors such as a wrong turn or click have consequences.

r002.rationale: The response compares the browser with a simulated environment and notes differences in their action spaces, but it does not state that web agents avoid challenges caused by physical presence in the world.

astra-6.text:
I think the connection is that, in both cases, you’re building an agent that has to act in an environment, observe what changes, and decide what to do next. It’s not just producing an answer in one shot. An action changes the context for the next action, and mistakes can compound over time.

That perspective makes you think about web agents as a closed-loop problem. If an agent clicks something, did it actually get to the page it expected? If it fills out a form, how does it know the information was accepted? You need to keep checking the state of the environment and be able to recover when things don’t go as planned.

It also shapes how you evaluate these systems. A plausible sequence of actions isn’t necessarily a successful sequence of actions. The question is whether the agent actually accomplished the user’s goal. So the lesson I’d carry over from embodied AI is to focus on that whole interaction loop—perception, action, feedback, and recovery—rather than treating planning alone as the problem.

r001.rationale: The response says both kinds of agents act in an environment, observe changes, and decide what to do next, with actions changing later context and mistakes compounding.

r002.rationale: It discusses the shared interaction loop but does not state that web agents avoid or remove challenges caused by physical presence in the world.

sol-6.1.text:
One thing that working in embodied AI has reinforced for us is the importance of closing the loop between perception and action. An agent takes an action, observes how the environment changes, and then decides what to do next. You can’t assume that your initial understanding is complete or that every action will have the intended effect.

That perspective carries over quite naturally to web agents. Instead of navigating a physical space, you’re navigating a website, but you still need to understand the current state, take an action, and check whether it moved you toward the goal. If you click something and the page changes unexpectedly, you need to recover rather than continue executing a plan that no longer makes sense.

It also shapes how we think about evaluation. Getting an individual action right is useful, but ultimately the question is whether the agent can complete a task over many steps, including when something goes wrong. That emphasis on interaction and recovery is a big part of what embodied AI brings to thinking about web agents.

r001.rationale: The response says agents act, observe how the environment changes, and decide what to do next, then applies that action-and-consequence loop to web agents.

r002.rationale: It contrasts navigating a website with navigating a physical space, but does not state that web-agent building removes many challenges caused by physical presence in the world.
